Save only works of piety, charity, and necessity. These are allowed by our Saviour. {Mar 2:23-28; Mar 3:4} The Jews superstitiously hold, {a} that it is not lawful for a blind man to lean upon a staff on a Sabbath day, as the lame may: that if a flea bite a man on that day, he may take it, but not kill it. That if a thorn prick him in the foot on that day, he may not pull it out. That a tailor may not carry a needle, much less a sword; that a man may not spet, {b} or be taken out of a jakes, as that Jew of Tewkesbury, who said,
paragraphs.anchor: Ye shall do no work therein.

paragraphs.anchor: And he shall wave the sheaf.

paragraphs.text: Here the Lord’s day was prefigured, saith one, therefore prescribed, and instituted of God. This shake day sheaf was a pregnant type of Christ’s rising again, the firstfruits from the dead. It was fulfilled in Christ’s resurrection, the day after the Sabbath. And because this Sabbath was chiefly meant of the Passover (which was a high Sabbath) it was a double Sabbath wherein Christ rested in the grave. The very next morning was Christ waved before the Lord, when, in the earthquake, he rose from the dead "the firstfruits of them that sleep," and there hence entered the everlasting gates as a King of glory, {Psa 24:7} which psalm is in the Greek called A psalm of David of the first day of the week.

paragraphs.text: That is, seven weeks. The Sabbath is queen of all the days of the week; and therefore carries the name of the whole week.
And then keep the feast of Pentecost or of weeks, so called because it was seven weeks after the passover.
That is, Out of the new corn (growing of the same land which God gave them to inherit) not foreign.
viz., Of their wheat harvest, as the shake sheaf {Lev 23:10} was of their barley harvest. Thus were they to express their thankfulness to God for those precious fruits of the earth. {Jas 5:7}
Besides which, they had other oblations at the feast of Pentecost. {Num 28:27} The service of God was heretofore very costly.

The siege of Jerusalem by the Romans lasted six months. It began at the passover, and ended at this feast of tabernacles. Ita festum illud fuit finis istius politiae.
